3710: A credenza is a long, low piece of furniture — essentially a storage cabinet — that sits flat against a wall. Think of it as a wide box, low to the ground, with a flat top and storage space (doors, drawers, or shelves) hidden below. That's the core of it.

Picture a piece of furniture that is:

  • Wide and horizontal — much longer than it is tall
  • Low — typically around 2 to 3 feet in height, noticeably shorter than a dining table
  • Flat on top — the surface is open and usable
  • Enclosed below — the space underneath has doors or drawers that hide the storage inside
  • Often raised slightly off the floor on short legs

The overall impression is of something sleek, compact, and hugging the wall rather than standing tall in the middle of a room.

A credenza is used in two main settings:

At home — most commonly in the dining room, living room, or an entryway. In a dining room, it plays the role of a serving and storage unit. You might set dishes on its flat top during a meal, and store extra cutlery, napkins, or table linens inside. In a living room, people place a TV on top of it and store media equipment or books behind its doors.

In an office — this is where the word is especially common today. An office credenza typically sits directly behind a person's desk, forming an L-shape or U-shape workspace. It gives the person extra surface area to spread out work, and the storage below holds files, office supplies, or equipment like a printer.

The credenza serves two purposes at once:

  1. Storage — keeping things organized and out of sight behind closed doors or drawers
  2. Surface space — the flat top acts as a shelf, display area, or extra workspace

This combination — hidden storage below, usable surface on top — is what makes a credenza useful. It keeps a room tidy while still giving you a surface to work with or display things on.
How it differs from similar furniture

You might wonder: isn't this just a cabinet or a sideboard? Here's how to tell them apart:

  • A regular cabinet is usually tall and upright, like a wardrobe or a bookcase. A credenza is deliberately low and wide — its horizontal, low profile is its defining feature.
  • A sideboard or buffet is very similar to a credenza. In fact, the words are often used interchangeably. If there is a distinction, a credenza tends to be slightly lower and sleeker, while a buffet or sideboard often implies a dining room piece used for serving food. In everyday conversation, the line between them is blurry.
  • A console table is also low and wall-hugging, but it is typically narrow (front to back), open underneath (no enclosed storage), and more decorative. A credenza has enclosed storage — that is the key difference.
  • A TV stand can look almost identical to a credenza. The word "credenza" is simply the more formal or furniture-world term for the same general shape when it's placed in an office or a living room.
The feel of the word in use

When someone says "credenza," they are usually pointing to something that looks deliberate and refined — not just a random box on the floor. In an office, a credenza signals a proper, organized workstation. In a home, it gives a room a polished, finished look. The word carries a slight tone of formality compared to, say, "cabinet" or "shelf."

You might hear it in sentences like:

  • "Put the printer on the credenza behind your desk."
  • "She arranged flowers on top of the credenza in the dining room."
  • "The mid-century modern credenza has become a popular interior design piece."

A credenza is a long, low, wall-side storage cabinet with a flat, usable top and enclosed storage below. It is found in both homes (dining rooms, living rooms) and offices (behind the desk). Its defining traits are its low height, wide horizontal shape, and the combination of hidden storage with an open top surface. When you see a sleek, low piece of furniture sitting against a wall with doors or drawers and things placed neatly on top — that is a credenza.
3711:
Credibility is the quality of being trusted and believed by others. When a person, organization, or source of information has credibility, people accept what they say as true and rely on what they do as dependable.

Think of it this way: if your friend has told you the truth every single time in the past, you will most likely believe them the next time they tell you something. That trust you have in them — that confidence that they are worth believing — is credibility. They have earned it.
The Most Important Thing to Understand About Credibility

Here is a crucial point that many people miss: credibility is not something you give yourself. It is something others give you.

You cannot wake up one morning and decide "I have credibility." Other people decide that for you, based on what they observe about you over time. You can work toward credibility, but only others can grant it to you. This is what makes credibility so valuable and so fragile.
What Credibility Is Made Of

Credibility is not one single thing. It is built from a combination of qualities that others observe in you:

Honesty is the foundation. If people catch you lying even once, your credibility takes a serious hit. A person who consistently tells the truth — even when it is inconvenient or uncomfortable — builds a reputation for being believable.

Competence matters just as much. A doctor who correctly diagnoses patients, a mechanic who fixes cars properly, or an economist who makes accurate predictions — these people build credibility because they know what they are doing and their results prove it. You are more likely to believe someone who is an expert in their field than someone who is not.

Consistency is what sustains credibility over time. If your words and your actions match each other, and if you behave the same way regardless of who is watching, people begin to see you as reliable and trustworthy. Inconsistency, on the other hand, makes people doubt you.

A track record is the accumulated proof. Over time, if someone has repeatedly told the truth, made correct judgments, and kept their promises, their credibility grows stronger. History matters. People look at your past behavior to predict your future behavior.
How Credibility Is Gained

Credibility is earned slowly, through repeated honest and competent behavior over time. It cannot be rushed. A journalist who consistently reports accurate stories builds credibility with readers over years. A scientist who conducts careful, well-reasoned research gains credibility within their field. A friend who keeps secrets and never breaks a promise earns your trust gradually.

It helps to be transparent — meaning, you are open about your reasoning, your sources, and your limitations. When people can see why you believe what you believe or how you arrived at a conclusion, they are more likely to trust you than if you simply demand to be believed.
How Credibility Is Lost

While credibility takes a long time to build, it can be destroyed very quickly. This is one of its most important characteristics.

Getting caught in a lie is the fastest way to destroy credibility, and the damage is often lasting. Once people know you have lied, they begin to question everything you have said before and everything you say after. The same applies to breaking promises, exaggerating facts, hiding important information, or being proven wrong repeatedly without acknowledging it.

A conflict of interest can also damage credibility. For example, if a food critic is secretly paid by a restaurant to write positive reviews, their opinions lose credibility even if what they wrote happened to be true — because people can no longer trust that their judgment is independent and honest.
Credibility Can Be Specific to a Subject

An important nuance: credibility is often domain-specific, meaning someone can have high credibility in one area and low credibility in another.

A famous athlete may have enormous credibility when talking about training and fitness, but that does not automatically give them credibility when they talk about economics or medicine. Treating someone as credible outside their area of expertise is a common mistake.
Credibility in Different Contexts

The word is used across many areas of life:

In everyday life, a person who is known to be honest and reliable has personal credibility. Others trust their word and their judgment.

In journalism and media, a news source has credibility when it reports facts accurately, corrects its errors publicly, and does not distort the truth. When a news organization repeatedly publishes false or misleading stories, it loses credibility and people stop trusting it as a source.

In science and research, credibility comes from rigorous methodology, honest reporting of results, and the ability for others to verify and reproduce findings. A scientist who fabricates data destroys not only their own credibility but potentially the credibility of their institution.

In politics and government, politicians and governments have credibility when their actions match their stated values and promises. A government that says one thing and does another suffers a credibility gap — a term used to describe the gulf between what an authority claims and what people actually believe. This term became well-known during the Vietnam War era when many Americans stopped believing what their government was telling them.

In business, a company's credibility with customers depends on delivering what it promises — reliable products, honest advertising, and good service. When companies mislead customers, they damage their credibility, often with lasting consequences.
The Credibility Gap — A Concept Worth Knowing

The credibility gap deserves a special mention because it appears often in discussions of politics, media, and institutions. It refers to the space between what someone says and what people actually believe. When a leader repeatedly makes promises that go unfulfilled, or when an institution's stated values are contradicted by its actions, a credibility gap forms. People stop taking the source at its word, even if what it says happens to be true on a given occasion. Closing a credibility gap is extremely difficult and requires sustained, demonstrable change in behavior over time.
Why Credibility Matters So Much

Credibility is essentially the currency of trust in human society. Without it, communication breaks down. If no one believes what you say, your words carry no weight. If no one trusts what you do, your actions have no influence.

For individuals, credibility shapes relationships, careers, and reputations. For organizations, it determines whether people rely on them. For governments, it defines the relationship between leadership and the public. For media and science, it is the very foundation of their purpose.
Related Word Forms

Since you may encounter this word in different forms, here is a quick guide:

Credible (adjective) — describes something or someone that has credibility. "She is a credible witness." "That is a credible explanation."

Credibly (adverb) — in a credible manner. "He credibly argued his case."

Incredible (adjective) — literally "not credible," meaning so extraordinary as to be hard to believe, though in modern everyday use it often simply means "amazing." "It was an incredible performance."

Incredibility (noun) — the state of being impossible or very hard to believe.
A Simple Way to Remember It

If you want one clean sentence to anchor the meaning in your mind:

Credibility is the earned reputation of being someone whose words can be trusted and whose competence can be relied upon — and it is always decided by others, never by yourself.
3712:
Credible means worthy of being believed. When something or someone is credible, you have solid, reasonable grounds to trust or believe them — not just a feeling, but actual backing from evidence, logic, track record, or expertise.

Think of it this way: if your very honest, careful friend tells you something happened, their account is credible. If a stranger with a history of lying tells you the same thing, their account is not credible. The event is the same. The believability is different.

"Credible" is used in two slightly different but closely related ways:

1. Believable and trustworthy
This is about a person, source, or piece of information being reliable enough to take seriously. It means: "I have good reason to trust this."

  • "She is a credible witness." → Her testimony can be trusted; she has no reason to lie, and her account is consistent.
  • "That is a credible news source." → It has a track record of accurate, well-researched reporting.
  • "He gave a credible explanation." → His explanation makes sense and is backed up by facts.

2. Convincing enough to be taken seriously as a real possibility
This sense is used especially with threats, claims, or plans. It means: "This is serious enough that it cannot be dismissed."

  • "The army issued a credible threat." → The threat is not empty; there is reason to believe it could actually be carried out.
  • "She made a credible case for changing the policy." → Her argument was strong enough to be genuinely considered.

Both senses share the same foundation: there is enough substance behind something for a reasonable person to take it seriously.
What Makes Something or Someone Credible?

Credibility doesn't come out of thin air. Something earns the label "credible" through one or more of these:

  • Evidence — It is supported by facts, data, or proof.
  • Consistency — The account doesn't contradict itself or other known facts.
  • Expertise or authority — The person speaking has genuine knowledge or training in the area.
  • Track record — The person or source has been honest and accurate in the past.
  • Motive (or lack of one) — The person has no obvious reason to lie or exaggerate.

When these factors are present, credibility is high. When they're absent, credibility collapses.

These words are close in meaning but are not exactly the same. Understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "credible."

Credible vs. Believable
Believable is a softer, more casual word. It simply means "easy to believe." A fictional story can be believable. But credible carries more weight — it implies that there is actual substance or grounding behind the claim, not just that it sounds plausible.

A well-written novel character might be believable, but not credible in a court of law.

Credible vs. Plausible
Plausible means "seeming reasonable or possible on the surface." Something plausible could be true. Something credible is more firmly grounded — it doesn't just seem possible, it has enough support to be genuinely trusted or taken seriously. Plausible is about surface appearance; credible goes deeper.

His alibi was plausible — it could have happened — but the detective didn't find it credible because the details didn't hold up under questioning.

Credible vs. Reliable
Reliable means consistently dependable over time. A reliable person always does what they say. Credible is specifically about being believable and trustworthy in what they say or claim, not necessarily about consistency over time.

A new doctor you've never met can be credible based on their qualifications, even though you have no personal history with them to call them reliable yet.

Credible vs. Trustworthy
Trustworthy is about the character of a person — they can be trusted in general. Credible is more specific to a particular claim, account, or statement being worthy of belief. You might find someone generally trustworthy but still not find their specific claim credible if the evidence doesn't support it.

When something or someone is not credible, a reasonable person would have good reasons to doubt or dismiss them. This can happen because:

  • The account contradicts known facts.
  • The person has an obvious motive to lie.
  • There is no supporting evidence.
  • The story keeps changing.
  • The person lacks any relevant knowledge or expertise.

"The committee found the witness's testimony not credible after it was shown to conflict with recorded footage."

The opposite of credible can be expressed as not credible, incredible (in its formal sense), or implausible, depending on the context.

Here are credible used across a wide range of real-world situations so you can see how the word behaves:

  • Journalism: "Always make sure your information comes from a credible source before publishing it."
  • Law: "The jury found the eyewitness credible because her account remained consistent throughout the trial."
  • Politics/Security: "The government responded only after intelligence confirmed a credible threat to national security."
  • Everyday life: "He offered a credible excuse — he had been in the hospital, and he showed us the paperwork."
  • Science: "The research team presented credible evidence linking the chemical to the disease."
  • Acting/Performance: "She delivered a credible performance as a grieving mother." (Here, it means convincing enough to be believed.)
  • Business: "For investors to fund your startup, you need a credible business plan backed by real numbers."

This is perhaps the most important thing to understand about the word.

Credible does not mean correct or true. It means worthy of belief given the available information. Something can be credible and still turn out to be wrong. A story can be not credible and still happen to be true.

A scientist might put forward a credible hypothesis — one backed by strong reasoning and early evidence — that is later disproved. It was still credible at the time.

Think of credibility as your reasonable judgement about whether to believe something, made with the information you currently have. Truth is the final reality. Credibility is your best assessment of it.

Credible means worthy of trust and belief, backed by enough evidence, logic, consistency, or authority that a reasonable person would take it seriously. It applies to people, statements, threats, evidence, sources, and arguments. It is stronger than "believable" or "plausible" because it implies genuine grounding, not just surface appeal. And critically, it is about the reasonableness of believing something, not a guarantee that it is true.
3713: The word credit is about trust. Nearly every meaning of this word, no matter how different they look on the surface, is rooted in the idea of one party trusting another — trusting that someone will pay back money, trusting that someone did the work, trusting that a claim is true. Once you see this thread, all the different meanings of the word fall into place naturally and permanently.
Meaning 1: The Ability to Borrow Money (Financial Credit)

This is the meaning most people encounter first. Credit, in its financial sense, is the ability to receive money, goods, or services now, with the understanding that you will pay for them later. The whole arrangement is built on trust — the lender trusts that you will keep your promise and pay back what you owe.

When a bank gives you credit, they are essentially saying: "We trust you enough to give you money today. You can pay us back over time."

Some important things that fall under this meaning:

Credit card: A card that lets you buy things immediately and pay the bill at the end of the month (or over time). The card company is extending credit — extending trust — to you.

Credit limit: The maximum amount of money a bank or lender will allow you to borrow. If your credit limit is $2,000, you cannot borrow more than that amount at one time.

Line of credit: A pre-approved pool of money that you can dip into whenever you need it, up to a set maximum. You only pay back what you actually use.

Credit score / Credit rating: A number (calculated by financial agencies) that represents how trustworthy you are as a borrower. It reflects your history of paying back debts. A high score tells lenders: "This person reliably pays their debts — trust them." A low score warns lenders: "This person has struggled to repay debts in the past — be cautious." Your credit score directly affects whether banks will lend you money and at what interest rate.

Good credit / Bad credit: If someone says you have good credit, it means you have a strong track record of repaying debts on time. Bad credit means the opposite — your history shows missed or late payments, making lenders less willing to trust you.

"On credit": When you buy something on credit, you take it now and pay later. Example: "She bought the furniture on credit."
Meaning 2: Credit in Accounting (A Formal Record Entry)

In the world of accounting — the system businesses use to track money — every single financial transaction is recorded in two parts: a debit and a credit. These are the two sides of every entry in a financial record book (called a ledger).

A credit in accounting means an entry that records money coming into an account, or a reduction in an amount owed. Think of it as the "good news" side for your bank account. When your employer deposits your salary into your account, the bank records it as a credit to your account — money has been added. You'll often see the abbreviation CR (for credit) on bank statements next to amounts that were deposited.

A debit, by contrast, records money going out.

This is also why when a company owes you money (say, for a refund or an overpayment), they may issue a credit note — a formal written document confirming that they owe you that amount.

Credit also means the acknowledgment, recognition, or praise that someone receives for something they have done or achieved. This meaning is extremely common in everyday conversation.

  • "She deserves all the credit for organizing the event." — She should be fully recognized and praised for it.
  • "He took the credit for the idea." — He claimed the recognition, whether or not he fully earned it.
  • "Give credit where credit is due." — A well-known saying that means you should fairly acknowledge people for their actual contributions, not overlook them.
  • "To your credit, you handled that situation with great patience." — This phrase means "something that reflects positively on you." It's a way of pointing out a quality or action that makes someone look good.

Notice how trust is still present here: when you give someone credit, you are publicly acknowledging — trusting — that they genuinely did the work or made the achievement.

In schools, colleges, and universities, a credit (sometimes called a credit hour) is a unit that measures the amount of coursework a student has successfully completed toward a degree or qualification.

Each course you pass earns you a certain number of credits. To graduate, a student typically needs to accumulate a required total number of credits — for example, 120 credits for a four-year university degree. The institution is essentially saying: "We confirm that this student completed this work."

  • "She earned 3 credits by completing that history course."
  • "He only needs 12 more credits to graduate."
Meaning 5: Film, TV, and Media Credits

When you stay until the end of a movie and a long list of names scrolls across the screen, those are called the credits — or more specifically, the end credits or closing credits. Each name listed is that person's credit: their official recognition for contributing to the production.

Credits can appear at the beginning of a film too — those are called opening credits, and they typically include the major names like the director, lead actors, and producers.

When someone says "She has 12 film credits," they mean she has officially contributed to 12 films and is listed in each of their credits.
Meaning 6: Belief in a Claim (Giving Credence)

Credit can also refer to the belief or trust you extend to a statement, claim, or story — in other words, how much you believe something.

  • "The new evidence gives more credit to his version of events." — It makes his account more believable.
  • "I wouldn't give much credit to those rumors." — I wouldn't believe them.
  • "The story gained more credit after the witnesses came forward." — The story became more believable.

Here, credit functions as a measure of believability. The more credit you give to a claim, the more you trust it to be true.

When you return a purchased item to a shop and the store doesn't refund your money in cash, they may offer you store credit instead. This is a set amount of money — held by the store — that you can use toward future purchases in that store only.

  • "I returned the coat and got $50 in store credit."

Store credit is not cash — it cannot be used elsewhere. It's simply the store's way of acknowledging that it owes you something.

Here is the beautiful part: if you look at all these meanings together, trust and acknowledgment are the common thread running through every single one:

Financial credit — A lender trusts you to repay borrowed money.
Accounting credit — A formal recorded entry showing money received or debt reduced.
Recognition — Publicly trusting and acknowledging that someone did the work.
Academic credit — An institution formally confirming that a student completed their studies.
Film credits — Officially listing and acknowledging everyone who contributed.
Belief in a claim — Extending trust to a statement or story.
Store credit — A shop's formal acknowledgment that it owes you money.

In every case, someone is either trusting that an obligation will be fulfilled, or acknowledging that something was done. That's the soul of the word. Whenever you encounter the word "credit" in a new context, ask yourself: Who is trusting whom? What is being acknowledged? The answer will almost always unlock the meaning immediately.
3714: "To credit" means to give recognition or acknowledgment to someone or something. Think of it as pointing at someone or something and saying, "This belongs to you" — whether that's praise, an achievement, a quality, money, or even just the truth of a story. That idea of "giving something its rightful place" runs through every meaning of this word.

1. To officially recognize someone as the person who did or created something (Attribution)

This is the most common use. When you credit someone, you publicly acknowledge them as the source, creator, or cause of something.

Examples:

  • "The film credits three writers for the screenplay." (acknowledges them officially)
  • "Scientists credited the breakthrough to decades of careful research." (recognized research as the cause)
  • "The director is credited as the producer as well." (officially listed)

Think of movie credits rolling on a screen — the word "credit" in that context comes directly from this verb form. Each person listed is being credited — publicly recognized for their contribution.

You can also credit a result to a cause (not just a person):

  • "The drop in crime was credited to the new policing strategy." (the strategy was recognized as the reason)

2. To believe or acknowledge that someone has a certain quality or ability

When you "credit someone with" a trait — like intelligence, honesty, or bravery — you are acknowledging that you believe they possess that quality.

Examples:

  • "Credit him with some common sense — he's not completely wrong." (acknowledge that he has common sense)
  • "I didn't credit her with enough courage to say that." (I didn't think she had enough courage)
  • "She credited her rival with more skill than he actually had." (she believed, perhaps wrongly, that he was more skilled)

Key tip: This construction is often used when someone is surprised by a quality, or when they are correcting an unfair assumption about someone. It can work as a gentle defense of someone:

  • "Give him some credit — at least he tried." (acknowledge his effort, don't ignore it)

3. To believe that something is true (formal use)

To "credit" a story, a claim, or a piece of information means to accept it as true, to find it believable. This is a more formal or literary use, but it appears in serious writing and formal speech.

Examples:

  • "It is difficult to credit such a wild story." (hard to believe)
  • "Few people credited his version of events." (few people believed him)
  • "Would you credit it? She actually finished the marathon!" (Can you believe it?)

The last example — "Would you credit it?" — is an exclamation of surprise, used to say "Can you believe this actually happened?" It's more common in British English.

4. To add money to a financial account (Banking/Accounting)

In banking, to credit an account means to put money into it — to add funds. This is the opposite of debit, which means to take money out.

Examples:

  • "The bank will credit your account within five business days." (add the money to your account)
  • "A refund of $50 has been credited to your account." (the $50 has been added)
  • "We will credit the amount directly to your balance." (place the money into your balance)

Simple way to remember: Debit = money leaves your account. Credit = money enters your account.

Note for deeper learners: In professional accounting, "credit" and "debit" have more technical meanings that can seem counterintuitive (for example, crediting a liability account increases it). But in everyday personal banking — which is what most people encounter — a credit always means money being added to your account.

Understanding how to build a sentence with "credit" as a verb is just as important as knowing what it means. Here are the patterns:

Pattern 1: credit + someone + with + something
(used for attribution and for acknowledging qualities)

  • "They credited her with the invention."
  • "I credit you with more wisdom than that."

Pattern 2: credit + something + to + someone
(used to attribute a result or achievement to a person or cause)

  • "She credited her success to hard work."
  • "The invention was credited to Newton."

Pattern 3: credit + account (financial)

  • "The bank credited my account."
  • "The money was credited to your account."

Pattern 4: credit + something (= believe)
(used with a story, claim, or fact as the object)

  • "I can't credit such a strange story."
  • "Nobody credited his explanation."
How to Tell the Meanings Apart in Context

Since the same word can mean different things, here is how to tell which meaning is being used:

  • If the sentence is about a bank, account, refund, or money → it means money is being added.
  • If the sentence is about a film, book, invention, discovery, or achievement → it means officially recognizing someone.
  • If the sentence is about a quality or ability (intelligence, patience, honesty) → it means acknowledging that someone has that quality.
  • If the sentence is about a story, claim, or report → it means believing it.

Knowing the opposite of a word locks its meaning in place:

  • In finance: the opposite is debit (taking money out).
  • In attribution: the opposite is discredit (to damage someone's reputation, or to deny them recognition) or to give blame (instead of recognition for something good).
  • In believing: the opposite is discredit or doubt (to not believe something).

To credit something or someone is to give rightful recognition — whether that means acknowledging who did something, believing someone has a quality, accepting something as true, or adding money to an account.
3715:
Creditable means deserving of praise, respect, or acknowledgment. When you call something creditable, you are saying it is good enough — or better than good enough — to earn recognition and admiration.

Think of it this way: if someone "deserves credit" for what they did, then what they did was creditable.

Creditable is a word of quiet, genuine approval. It doesn't scream brilliance or perfection — it says: "This is worthy of respect. This deserves to be acknowledged."

It is most commonly used when someone has done something well, especially under difficult conditions or against expectations. There is often an undertone of: "Given the circumstances, this was genuinely impressive and praiseworthy."

For example:

  • A young tennis player competing against a former champion loses, but played extremely well. → Her performance was creditable.
  • A small company competes in a market dominated by giants and holds its ground. → That is a creditable achievement.
  • A student with very limited resources writes a thorough, well-reasoned essay. → It is a creditable piece of work.

In each case, the thing being described earns genuine respect and commendation.
What creditable does NOT mean — critical distinctions

This is the most important section, because creditable is one of the most frequently confused words in English. It looks and sounds similar to several other words, but it means something entirely different from all of them.

Creditable ≠ Credible

This is the most common confusion.

  • Credible means believable or trustworthy. A credible witness is one you can believe. A credible threat is one that seems real and serious.
  • Creditable means praiseworthy or worthy of recognition. A creditable performance is one that deserves admiration.

These two words have almost nothing to do with each other in meaning, even though they look alike. Never use one when you mean the other.

✗ "She gave a credible performance at the concert." ← This would mean her performance was believable, which is a strange thing to say about a concert.
✓ "She gave a creditable performance at the concert." ← This means her performance was praiseworthy.

✗ "He is a creditable source of information." ← This would mean he deserves praise for being a source, which makes no sense here.
✓ "He is a credible source of information." ← This means he is trustworthy and believable.

Creditable ≠ Credulous

  • Credulous means too willing to believe things; gullible. A credulous person gets fooled easily because they believe almost anything.
  • Creditable has nothing to do with gullibility.

Creditable ≠ Discreditable

  • Discreditable is the direct opposite of creditable. It means bringing shame, disgrace, or loss of respect. A discreditable act is one that harms your reputation.

Creditable sits in an interesting position. It is a word of genuine, sincere praise — but it does not always mean exceptional or outstanding. Sometimes it simply means: good enough to deserve respect and recognition, even if not perfect or spectacular.

This is why you'll often see it in sentences like:

  • "It was a creditable effort, though there is room for improvement."
  • "The team put up a creditable showing against the tournament favourites."

In such sentences, the speaker is sincerely praising what was done, but is also gently acknowledging that it was perhaps not flawless. It is honest approval — not hollow flattery, and not faint praise either.

However, creditable can also simply describe something genuinely impressive without any qualification:

  • "She has had a long and creditable career in public service."

Here, it means her career is genuinely admirable and worthy of recognition — full stop.

Creditable is a moderately formal word. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Written reviews or assessments ("a creditable debut novel")
  • Formal reports or evaluations ("the team delivered a creditable result")
  • Commentary on sports, arts, or professional performance ("a creditable display from the home side")

In casual everyday speech, people more often just say "impressive," "praiseworthy," "commendable," or "well done." But in writing, or in more formal spoken contexts, creditable is precise and elegant.

Creditable = worthy of praise and recognition; deserving of credit for what was done.

If something is creditable, it earns genuine respect and acknowledgment — it is the kind of thing people should rightly give you credit for.
3716:
A credo is a personal statement of core beliefs — a declaration of the things you believe so deeply that they shape how you live, work, and make decisions.

Think of it this way: if someone asked you, "What do you truly stand for? What principles do you refuse to abandon no matter what?" — your honest, thoughtful answer to that question would be your credo.

It's important to understand that a credo is not just any belief. Everyone believes hundreds of things. A credo is different because:

  • It is foundational — it sits at the very core of who you are or what an organization represents.
  • It is guiding — it actively directs your choices and behavior in life.
  • It is committed — it is not casual or temporary. It is something you genuinely stand behind.
  • It is often expressed openly — written down, declared, or communicated to others.

So while you might believe that coffee is better than tea, that is obviously not a credo. A credo would be something like: "I believe every human being deserves dignity and respect, regardless of their background." That belief runs deep, defines your character, and influences how you treat people every single day.

A person's credo is the set of values and principles they live by. It answers the question: "What do I genuinely believe, and how does that belief guide my life?"

Here are a few examples of what a personal credo might look like:

  • "I believe in hard work, honesty, and never asking others to do what I am unwilling to do myself."
  • "I believe that kindness costs nothing and changes everything."
  • "I believe in taking full responsibility for my actions and never blaming others for my circumstances."

Notice that a credo is deeply personal and specific. It reflects a person's character, values, and worldview. Two people can share some beliefs but have very different credos overall.

A credo is not limited to individuals. Organizations — companies, institutions, movements — can also have a credo. In this context, it is a public declaration of the values and responsibilities the organization commits to upholding.

One of the most famous examples is Johnson & Johnson's Credo, a formal written document the company has followed since 1943. It states that the company's first responsibility is to doctors, nurses, and patients — and that profit comes last, not first. This credo has guided how the company makes decisions for decades.

When an organization has a credo, it signals to the world: "This is what we stand for. Judge us by this."
How a Credo Differs from Similar Words

Since several words feel similar to "credo," it helps to understand how they differ:

Credo vs. Belief: A belief is a single thing you accept as true. A credo is a collection of core beliefs, organized into a meaningful statement that defines your identity or direction. Your credo is made up of beliefs, but it is bigger than any single one.

Credo vs. Motto: A motto is typically a short, catchy phrase — like "Just Do It" or "Never Give Up." A credo is fuller and more substantial. It explains what you believe and why, not just a slogan.

Credo vs. Creed: These two words are extremely close in meaning and are often interchangeable. The difference is mainly in feel and context. Creed tends to be used in more religious or formal settings (like a church's statement of faith). Credo can be used in both religious and everyday secular contexts, and it carries a slightly more personal, individual tone.

Credo vs. Mission Statement: A mission statement tells you what an organization does or where it is going — its purpose or goal. A credo tells you what it believes and values — the principles behind its actions. A mission statement is about direction; a credo is about character.

Credo vs. Philosophy: A philosophy is a broad, elaborate system of thought about life, knowledge, and existence. A credo is more focused and practical — it is a distilled, personal commitment to specific beliefs, intended to guide real-world behavior.

The word "credo" has a long history in religious contexts. In Christianity, it refers to a formal declaration of faith — a statement of what believers accept as true about God, Jesus Christ, and salvation. The most well-known examples are the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed, which have been recited in Christian worship for centuries. These are precise, structured statements that define the core beliefs of the faith.

This religious usage is where the word originally carried its most serious weight — to declare a credo in this context meant stating the non-negotiable beliefs you were willing to stake your entire spiritual life on.

Over time, the word moved into everyday secular life, keeping that same sense of deep commitment and seriousness, just applied to personal or organizational values rather than religious doctrine.
The Key Qualities of Any Credo

Whether personal, organizational, or religious, every genuine credo shares these qualities:

It is sincere. A credo is not a performance or a marketing tool. It reflects what someone truly believes, not what sounds impressive.

It is stable. A credo does not change with the wind. It remains consistent across time and circumstances, which is what gives it authority and meaning.

It is actionable. A credo is not just a thought — it leads to action. You can look at how a person or organization actually behaves and ask, "Are they living their credo?"

It is defining. A credo reveals character. It tells you something fundamental about who a person or organization truly is.

Here are some natural examples of the word in use:

  • "Her credo has always been to leave every situation better than she found it."
  • "The founder built the entire company around a simple credo: treat every customer as a trusted friend."
  • "His personal credo — that failure is just unfinished success — kept him going through every setback."
  • "The team adopted a credo of radical transparency, where nothing important would ever be hidden from anyone."

The plural of credo is credos (sometimes also spelled credoes, though credos is more common today).

In short, a credo is a statement of deeply held beliefs that defines who you are or what you stand for, and that actively guides how you live or operate. It is serious, stable, and sincere — not a passing opinion, but a true declaration of your core principles.
3717:
Credulity is the tendency to believe things too easily, too quickly, and without asking for good reasons or evidence.

A person with credulity does not stop to question whether something is true. They simply hear a claim and accept it. Think of it as a kind of mental door that swings open too freely — almost anything can walk right in, no matter how unlikely or unproven.

Imagine someone tells you they have a magic cream that cures any illness overnight, and you immediately believe them and buy it — without asking for proof, without being suspicious, without wondering if it's too good to be true. That willingness to believe without checking is credulity.

Credulity is not about one single moment of being fooled. It is a tendency — a general habit or quality of mind that makes a person consistently easy to persuade. It describes how readily someone gives their belief away.
The Tone: Is It a Good or Bad Word?

Almost always negative or critical. When someone uses the word "credulity," they are usually pointing out a weakness — a lack of critical thinking, a failure to question things properly.

Saying someone "has great credulity" is not a compliment. It means they are dangerously easy to deceive.

The only gentle exception is when referring to children, who are naturally credulous (believing in Santa Claus, for example). In that context, credulity is seen as innocent rather than foolish.

Credulity exists on a scale:

Low credulity — A person who is slightly more trusting than average, maybe open-minded to unusual ideas. Mostly harmless.

High credulity — A person who swallows almost everything they hear. They are easily exploited by scammers, manipulators, cult leaders, and bad-faith salespeople.

The higher the credulity, the more vulnerable the person is to being deceived.

Here is where you will typically encounter this word:

  • Con artists and scammers exploit the credulity of their victims to extract money.
  • Conspiracy theories spread because of the credulity of people who share them without fact-checking.
  • Cult leaders seek out people with high credulity, as these individuals are more likely to follow without questioning.
  • Fake news thrives wherever credulity is widespread in a population.
  • Advertising often relies on mild credulity — the willingness of consumers to believe exaggerated claims.

These are set expressions you will encounter in writing and conversation:

"Strain credulity" or "stretch credulity"
This means something is so far-fetched or unbelievable that it tests the limits of even a very trusting person's willingness to believe.
Example: "The company claimed their pill could make you fluent in French in three days — a claim that strains credulity."

"Beggar credulity"
This is a stronger version. Something "beggars credulity" when it is so outrageous that it utterly defies belief — it exhausts even the most credulous person's capacity to believe.
Example: "The politician's excuse for his absence beggared credulity."

Here are sentences that show the word used naturally:

  1. The fraudster made millions by exploiting the credulity of elderly people who trusted him completely.
  2. Her credulity was such that she believed every rumour she heard at work.
  3. Children have a natural credulity that makes fairy tales feel completely real to them.
  4. The advertisement beggared credulity — no pill can make you lose 10 kilograms in a week.
  5. The journalist warned that public credulity was allowing misinformation to go viral.

Credulous (adjective) — This is the describing word. A credulous person is one who has credulity. If credulity is the noun (the quality), credulous describes the person possessing it.
"She was so credulous that she sent money to a stranger who claimed to be a prince."

Credulously (adverb) — Describes the manner in which someone believes something.
"He credulously accepted everything the salesman told him."

Incredulity (noun) — The opposite of credulity. It is the unwillingness or inability to believe something. Where credulity is a door flung wide open, incredulity is a door firmly locked.
"He stared at the magician with complete incredulity, unable to understand what he had just witnessed."

Incredulous (adjective) — Describing a person or expression showing disbelief.
"She gave him an incredulous look when he said he'd won the lottery."
How Credulity Differs from Similar Words

These words are close neighbours, but they are not identical:

Gullibility — The closest cousin to credulity. Gullibility tends to emphasise being easily tricked or deceived — it leans towards the action of being fooled. Credulity is broader; it is more about the general tendency to believe too easily, whether or not you are actively being tricked. In everyday use, though, they are nearly interchangeable and both carry a negative tone.

Naivety — Being naive means being innocent, inexperienced, and unsophisticated. A naive person may believe things easily because they lack experience with how the world works. Credulity is less about innocence and more about a habit of not questioning. You can be naive without being credulous, and credulous without being naive (a worldly adult can still have high credulity).

Trust — Trust is not negative. Trust is a reasoned or earned willingness to rely on someone. Credulity is unearned, uncritical belief in something without good reason. Trust is a virtue; credulity is a weakness.

Faith — Faith refers to belief without material proof, usually in a spiritual or religious context. It carries respect and dignity. Credulity, by contrast, is never a respectful term — it implies poor judgment, not devotion.
If you had to remember just one thing: credulity is the quality of believing things too easily, without enough questioning or evidence — and it is almost always seen as a flaw.
3718:
Credulous means too willing to believe things, especially without questioning whether they are true or asking for proof.

A credulous person hears a claim and accepts it easily — often because they simply trust what others say, without stopping to think critically or ask, "Is this actually true? What's the evidence?"

Think of it this way: the world has a spectrum of how much people question things before believing them.

On one end, you have the skeptic — someone who questions everything, demands evidence, and is hard to convince. On the other end, you have the credulous person — someone who is very easy to convince, asks few questions, and rarely doubts what they're told.

Being credulous doesn't mean a person is stupid. It simply means their mental guard is low. They give their belief away too easily, like a person who opens their front door to a stranger without checking who it is first.

Credulous carries a mildly negative tone. When you call someone credulous, you're gently criticizing their lack of careful thinking. You're suggesting they should be more careful about what they choose to believe.

It is not a harsh or insulting word, but it is not a compliment either. It implies a kind of intellectual vulnerability — a tendency to be misled or deceived simply because the person didn't pause to evaluate a claim.
Credulous vs. Words It's Easily Confused With

Credulous vs. Gullible
These two words are very close in meaning, and in everyday use, people treat them as almost identical. However, gullible is slightly stronger and more informal. A gullible person doesn't just believe easily — they are easily tricked or fooled, often as a result. Credulous is the more formal, neutral word that focuses on the belief itself, while gullible highlights the consequence of that belief (being deceived). All gullible people are credulous, but a credulous person may not always end up being fooled.

Credulous vs. Trusting
Trusting is a neutral or even positive word. A trusting person has faith in others, which is generally a good quality in close relationships. Credulous, however, suggests the trust is indiscriminate — applied to anyone and anything, even when caution is needed. Being trusting with your close friends is healthy; being credulous with a stranger selling you something suspicious is a problem.

Credulous vs. Naive
Naive is broader — it means a general lack of worldly experience or sophistication. A naive person may be credulous as a result of their inexperience, but naivety covers more than just believing things easily. You can be naive about how the business world works, how relationships function, etc. Credulous specifically refers to the act of believing claims without sufficient questioning.

Here are examples that show the word working naturally in sentences:

  • "She was so credulous that when her coworker told her the office was closing early as a prank, she immediately packed up her bag and left."

Here, she believed the claim without verifying it.

  • "Advertisers love credulous consumers — people who see a bold health claim on a product and buy it without researching whether it's actually true."

Here, credulousness leads to being easily influenced.

  • "He wasn't a fool, but he was credulous by nature — he always assumed people were telling him the truth."

Here, the word is used with some empathy, acknowledging that credulousness can come from a place of natural goodness (believing the best in others), not foolishness.

  • "The cult grew rapidly because it targeted credulous individuals who were going through difficult times and desperately wanted to believe in something."

Here, credulousness is seen as a vulnerability that was exploited.

The direct opposite of credulous is incredulous, which means unwilling or unable to believe something — shocked that something could even be true. If someone tells you an outrageous story and you respond with wide eyes saying "That can't be real," you are being incredulous.

Other opposites in spirit include: skeptical, doubtful, cynical, and questioning.
A Simple Way to Always Remember It

Imagine a child who believes everything adults tell them — that Santa Claus is real, that eating carrots improves your eyesight, that if you swallow a watermelon seed a watermelon will grow in your stomach. That child, in that moment, is being credulous. As adults, we're expected to outgrow that and develop a habit of questioning claims before accepting them. When an adult still has that child-like habit of believing without questioning — especially in situations where they should be more careful — we call them credulous.

Credulous describes someone who is too quick and too willing to believe things, often without stopping to question, verify, or think critically — making them easy to mislead, whether intentionally or not.
3719:
A creed is a clearly defined set of beliefs or principles that a person or group holds as absolutely fundamental — the core convictions they live by, stand by, and identify with.

Think of it this way: if someone asked you, "What do you truly believe in? What guides your life?" — your honest, considered answer would be your creed.
What makes something a "creed" and not just a "belief"?

Not every belief qualifies as a creed. A creed has specific qualities that set it apart:

It is foundational. A creed isn't a casual or surface-level opinion. It's a belief that sits at the very core of who you are or what a group stands for. It shapes how you think, act, and make decisions. If someone challenges your creed, it doesn't just make you reconsider — it feels like a challenge to your whole identity.

It is defining. A creed tells you (and others) who a person or group is. It answers the question: "What does this person or group fundamentally stand for?"

It is stable. A creed isn't easily changed or abandoned. Unlike an opinion you might change after a single conversation, a creed is something you hold firmly over time.

It is often expressible. A creed can usually be stated — put into clear words. It might be a single sentence or a short list of principles. This is actually where the word gets much of its power: a creed is something you can declare.
The two main contexts where "creed" is used

1. Religious creeds

This is the oldest and most formal use of the word. In religion, a creed is an official, written summary of what members of a faith believe. It's a statement of doctrine — the essential truths of the religion, compressed into a form that can be recited, memorized, and declared.

The most well-known examples come from Christianity: the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed. These are short, formal statements that summarize the core Christian beliefs about God, Jesus, and salvation. When a Christian recites one of these in a church service, they are publicly declaring: this is what I believe.

But the use of creeds isn't unique to Christianity. Many religions have their own versions — formal declarations of faith that define the community and its beliefs.

2. Personal and secular creeds

Outside of religion, "creed" is also used in everyday life to refer to someone's personal guiding principles — the convictions that drive their behavior.

For example:

  • "His creed was simple: treat others the way you want to be treated."
  • "Her creed in business was: never compromise on quality."
  • "The organization's creed put honesty above everything else."

Here, a creed acts like an internal compass. It's not necessarily written down or officially declared, but it's real and it steers a person's choices consistently.
Creed vs. similar words — understanding the differences

These words are close relatives, but they are not interchangeable:

Creed vs. belief: A belief is a single thing you hold to be true. A creed is a set of core beliefs — organized, foundational, and identity-defining. All creeds are made of beliefs, but not all beliefs are part of a creed.

Creed vs. opinion: An opinion is often flexible and open to change with new information. A creed is firm — it isn't something you update after reading an article. Opinions are lightweight; creeds carry weight.

Creed vs. values: Values are the things you consider important or good (honesty, kindness, hard work). A creed often includes your values, but it goes further — it also includes what you believe to be true, not just what you believe to be good.

Creed vs. ideology: An ideology is a broad, systematic set of ideas — usually political or social — about how the world works and how society should be organized. A creed is more personal and more intimate. It's less about a theory of society and more about what you stand for, at your core.

Creed vs. doctrine: Doctrine is the official teaching of an institution (a church, a school of thought, a political party). A creed is often a condensed, declared version of that doctrine — the most essential parts, stated plainly. In religious contexts, doctrine is the full body of teachings; the creed is the distilled declaration.
An important nuance: creed as a synonym for religion or faith

In a broader sense, "creed" is sometimes used to mean an entire religion or faith tradition itself — not just its stated beliefs, but the whole system.

You'll often see it in phrases like:

  • "People of every race and creed"
  • "Regardless of creed or color"

Here, "creed" simply means "religion" or "faith." It's used to signal respect for religious diversity — acknowledging that different people follow different faiths, all of which deserve equal dignity.

"Creed" carries a slightly formal, even solemn weight. It's a word that signals seriousness. When you say someone has a creed, you're implying that their beliefs aren't casual — they are commitments. This is why the word appears often in formal, dignified contexts: religious ceremonies, organizational mission statements, inspirational writing, and declarations of principle.

If someone tells you their creed, they are trusting you with something important — not just what they think, but who they are.

A creed is a set of core, foundational beliefs or principles that define who a person or group is and guide how they live. It can be religious — a formal declaration of faith — or personal — the driving convictions behind someone's life and choices. What makes it a creed and not just a belief or an opinion is its depth, its stability, and the way it shapes identity. It is something you don't just hold in your mind; you live it.
